title: Imitation, Canon and Fugue
intro: When one voice repeats a melody that another has just played, the music is imitative. Canons repeat strictly; fugues build a whole piece from one subject entering in every voice.

blocks.text: Imitation is a voice repeating another's melody, usually starting a few beats later and often at a different pitch (at the fifth or the octave). It ties a texture together: each new voice is heard as related to the first.

A canon is strict imitation from beginning to end: the follower (comes) copies the leader (dux) exactly, at a fixed distance in time and pitch. Rounds such as 'Frère Jacques' and 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat' are canons at the unison where every voice can loop. Composers also wrote canons by inversion (the follower turns the melody upside down), by augmentation (twice as slow) and retrograde (backwards); Bach's Goldberg Variations include a canon at every interval from the unison to the ninth.

examples.label: Two voices, the second two bars behind

blocks.text: A fugue is a contrapuntal piece built on one theme, the subject. Its usual course:

items: Exposition: the subject enters in each voice in turn. The second entry, the answer, is the subject transposed to the dominant (a real answer is exact; a tonal answer adjusts a note or two so the music stays in the home key). While a new voice states the subject, the previous voice continues with a countersubject, a counter-melody designed to fit it.
Episodes: passages without a complete subject, usually sequences built from fragments of it, which modulate to related keys.
Middle entries: the subject returns in other keys.
Stretto: entries overlap, a new one starting before the last has finished, raising the intensity near the end.
Pedal point and final entry in the tonic: often over a held bass note, closing the piece.

blocks.text: Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier has a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key (two books, 48 pairs). The Fugue in C minor, BWV 847, is a compact three-voice model: the exposition, episodes built from the subject's head, and a final entry over a tonic pedal.

To learn a fugue, practise each voice alone, then every pair of voices, before playing all of them. Fingering is often unusual because one hand has to sustain one voice while moving another; pianists divide middle voices between the hands where that keeps every line legato.

blocks.title: Tonal answer
blocks.text: A fugue subject in C major begins C–G, the tonic leaping up to the dominant. What are the usual first two notes of a tonal answer, and why not a real answer?
solution: A real answer would transpose C–G up a fifth to G–D, which pulls towards G major too early. A tonal answer replies to the tonic–dominant leap with dominant–tonic: G–C. So the answer starts G–C and then continues as an exact transposition.

Yale University Press; Jeppesen, K. (1939). Counterpoint: The Polyphonic Vocal Style of the Sixteenth Century. Prentice-Hall (Dover reprint 1992).
